caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Nisha Kapoor is a 25-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks of pregnancy who presents to the antenatal unit with persistent nausea and vomiting for the last several days. She reports that she is unable to tolerate food and has kept down only small sips of water. She feels dizzy on standing, has a dry mouth, and says her clothes feel loose because she has been losing weight.
On assessment, the nurse notes blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, pulse 112 beats per minute, dry mucous membranes, dark concentrated urine, and visible fatigue. The patient says, “I wanted this pregnancy so much, but I feel miserable and weak all the time.” The nurse suspects hyperemesis gravidarum rather than normal morning sickness.

questions.prompt: Which findings most strongly support hyperemesis gravidarum rather than common nausea of pregnancy? Select all that apply.

options.A: Persistent vomiting with poor intake
options.B: Dizziness and weakness
options.D: Tachycardia and low blood pressure
options.E: Dry mucous membranes

questions.rationale: All these cues point to clinically significant fluid volume deficit rather than ordinary early-pregnancy nausea. Hyperemesis gravidarum is characterised by persistent vomiting, dehydration, weight loss, and hemodynamic changes. Dark urine and dry mucous membranes indicate poor hydration, while tachycardia and hypotension suggest the body is compensating for low circulating volume.

questions.prompt: What is the nurse’s priority interpretation of this presentation?

options.A: Normal first-trimester discomfort that can be managed by reassurance alone
options.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum with dehydration and risk of electrolyte imbalance
options.D: A psychiatric cause of vomiting with no obstetric significance

questions.rationale: This patient’s findings show more than common morning sickness. The signs of dehydration and likely electrolyte loss make this an obstetric and medical concern. NCLEX reasoning requires distinguishing expected pregnancy discomforts from findings that threaten maternal wellbeing and fetal support.

questions.prompt: Which problem should the nurse prioritise first?

options.A: Deficient fluid volume related to persistent vomiting
options.B: Fear related to pregnancy adjustment
options.D: Disturbed body image

questions.rationale: Although emotional support is important, the most urgent issue is fluid deficit. Dehydration can quickly worsen maternal perfusion, renal function, and nutritional status, which in turn may compromise pregnancy progress.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Begin focused assessment of hydration status, support rest, and prepare for fluid replacement and antiemetic therapy as prescribed
options.B: Encourage the patient to eat a heavy meal immediately
options.C: Tell the patient that vomiting is normal and she should go home
options.D: Delay intervention until the next prenatal visit

questions.rationale: Immediate nursing care should focus on hydration, safety, and preparation for treatment. Forcing a heavy meal is unrealistic and may worsen symptoms. Sending the patient home without treatment would ignore signs of dehydration and clinical deterioration.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Monitor intake and output closely
options.B: Reassess weight trends and urine concentration
options.C: Observe for worsening dizziness or electrolyte-related weakness
options.D: Provide nonjudgmental support and explain the condition
options.E: Ignore emotional distress because physical issues are the only priority

questions.rationale: NGN-level maternity care includes both physical and emotional support. Intake/output and weight trends help evaluate hydration and nutrition. Emotional reassurance matters because prolonged vomiting can be frightening and discouraging. Ignoring distress would not reflect holistic nursing care.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates that the plan of care is effective?

options.A: The patient tolerates fluids better, urine becomes less concentrated, pulse slows, and dizziness decreases
options.B: Vomiting worsens and the patient becomes more hypotensive
options.C: The nurse stops monitoring after one dose of antiemetic
options.D: The patient remains unable to take in fluids but says she feels hopeful

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by better hydration, less concentrated urine, more stable vital signs, and reduced dizziness. Hopefulness is valuable, but physiological improvement is the clearest outcome indicator.

caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Farah Ahmed is a 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks’ gestation who presents to the labour assessment unit complaining of a severe frontal headache, blurred vision, and sudden swelling of her hands and face. She reports that the baby has been moving, but she feels unusually unwell and says, “My head feels like it will burst.”
Assessment reveals blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, brisk reflexes, +3 protein on dipstick, and mild right upper quadrant discomfort. The fetal monitor is applied, and the nurse recognises that this pattern is concerning for severe preeclampsia with risk of maternal and fetal deterioration.

questions.prompt: Which findings are red flags for severe preeclampsia? Select all that apply.

options.A: Severe headache
options.B: Visual disturbance
options.D: Proteinuria and brisk reflexes
options.E: Right upper quadrant discomfort

questions.rationale: All of these are classic warning signs of severe preeclampsia. Headache, visual disturbance, and hypertension suggest cerebral involvement. Brisk reflexes indicate increased neuromuscular irritability, and right upper quadrant pain may reflect hepatic involvement. NCLEX-style maternity questions place heavy emphasis on recognising these as urgent findings.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation of this presentation?

options.A: Normal third-trimester discomforts
options.B: Severe preeclampsia with risk of seizure, placental compromise, and maternal organ injury
options.D: Early postpartum haemorrhage

questions.rationale: The symptom cluster is highly concerning for severe preeclampsia. This is not an expected discomfort of pregnancy. The nurse must think about maternal cerebral, renal, hepatic, and placental risks.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Risk for maternal seizure and reduced placental perfusion
options.B: Disturbed sleep pattern
options.D: Anxiety about motherhood

questions.rationale: The priority is prevention of maternal and fetal injury. Preeclampsia threatens the brain, liver, kidneys, and uteroplacental circulation. That risk overrides all long-term teaching needs.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Reduce stimulation, maintain safety, initiate close maternal-fetal monitoring, and prepare for urgent antihypertensive and magnesium sulfate therapy as prescribed
options.B: Encourage the patient to walk around to reduce swelling
options.C: Offer a large meal and discharge home
options.D: Delay intervention until laboratory results return next day

questions.rationale: The nurse must reduce seizure risk, support close monitoring, and prepare for time-sensitive management. Walking, discharge, or delay would be unsafe. In severe preeclampsia, nursing priorities include seizure precautions, fetal assessment, and readiness for urgent escalation.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Monitor reflexes, respiratory status, and urine output closely if magnesium sulfate is started
options.B: Assess fetal heart rate patterns and maternal symptoms frequently
options.D: Dismiss blurred vision because oedema alone explains it
options.E: Prepare for possible urgent birth if maternal or fetal status worsens

questions.rationale: Magnesium sulfate monitoring is critical because toxicity can depress respirations. Fetal monitoring remains essential because placental perfusion may be impaired. Visual changes should never be dismissed in preeclampsia. Anticipating possible urgent delivery reflects advanced clinical judgment.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates improvement or stabilisation?

options.A: Blood pressure becomes better controlled, severe headache lessens, reflexes are appropriately monitored, and fetal status remains reassuring
options.B: Headache intensifies and blood pressure rises further
options.C: Respirations fall dangerously on magnesium sulfate without reassessment
options.D: Fetal monitoring is discontinued because the mother feels calmer

questions.rationale: Stabilisation is shown by improved blood pressure, reduced neurological symptoms, and continued maternal-fetal monitoring. Respiratory depression or worsening hypertension would indicate poor control or complications.

caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Simran Kaur is a 29-year-old woman at 35 weeks’ gestation admitted earlier in the day with severe preeclampsia. While the nurse is updating observations, the patient suddenly becomes rigid and begins to seize in bed. Her partner panics and calls for help.
The fetal monitor is in place, the room has low lighting, and side rails are raised. The nurse must protect the mother from injury, support airway safety, and prepare for emergency management while recognising that fetal compromise may also occur during the event.

questions.prompt: What makes this an obstetric emergency? Select all that apply.

options.A: Tonic-clonic seizure activity
options.B: Known severe preeclampsia
options.D: Maternal risk of airway compromise and trauma
options.E: Possible fetal compromise during maternal seizure

questions.rationale: A seizure in a patient with severe preeclampsia is eclampsia, a life-threatening obstetric emergency. Pregnancy context is important, but what makes the situation emergent is the direct risk to maternal airway, oxygenation, circulation, and fetal wellbeing.

questions.prompt: What is the nurse’s priority interpretation?

options.A: The patient is having a normal labour event
options.B: The patient is experiencing eclampsia requiring immediate seizure management and maternal-fetal stabilisation
options.C: The patient only needs comfort measures
options.D: The seizure can be ignored until it stops

questions.rationale: This is eclampsia and must be treated urgently. NCLEX expects immediate recognition of seizure risk in hypertensive pregnancy complications and rapid implementation of emergency priorities.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent during the seizure?

options.A: Airway obstruction, maternal injury, and decreased oxygen delivery to mother and fetus
options.B: Disturbed sleep pattern
options.D: Anxiety about labour pain

questions.rationale: During active seizure, the greatest danger is compromise of maternal airway, oxygenation, and physical safety. The fetus is also vulnerable if maternal oxygen delivery drops.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Stay with the patient, protect from injury, position for airway safety as feasible after the seizure, call for urgent help, and prepare prescribed seizure management
options.B: Put an object in the patient’s mouth to prevent tongue injury
options.C: Try to hold the patient down forcefully
options.D: Leave the room to find the doctor before doing anything else

questions.rationale: The nurse must remain with the patient, protect from injury, and support airway safety. Objects should never be forced into the mouth. Forceful restraint can injure the patient. Leaving the room without first ensuring active response and protection would be unsafe.

questions.prompt: Which additional actions are appropriate after the seizure subsides? Select all that apply.

options.A: Reassess airway, breathing, circulation, and maternal level of consciousness
options.B: Assess fetal status and continue close monitoring
options.C: Prepare for magnesium sulfate or review of ongoing magnesium therapy as ordered
options.D: Maintain seizure precautions and low stimulation
options.E: Assume no further assessment is needed once the shaking stops

questions.rationale: Post-seizure care includes full maternal reassessment, fetal reassessment, seizure prevention strategies, and medication management. The end of visible seizure activity does not mean the emergency has ended.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates that immediate nursing management is effective?

options.A: The mother is protected from injury, airway is maintained, maternal status is reassessed, and fetal monitoring resumes appropriately
options.B: The patient remains unmonitored after the seizure ends
options.C: The nurse documents only the duration without reassessment
options.D: Fetal status is ignored because the seizure is over

questions.rationale: Effective care includes protection during the seizure and comprehensive reassessment afterward. Both mother and fetus require continued evaluation.

caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Elena D’Souza is a 33-year-old woman at 32 weeks’ gestation who presents with sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. She denies abdominal pain or contractions and says the baby has been moving normally. She appears frightened and asks whether her baby is in danger.
Her blood pressure is 110/68 mmHg, pulse 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and the bleeding continues lightly onto the pad. The nurse suspects placenta previa and understands that some common examination approaches are unsafe until the placenta location is confirmed.

questions.prompt: Which findings are most consistent with placenta previa? Select all that apply.

options.A: Bright-red vaginal bleeding
options.B: Painless bleeding
options.D: Absence of abdominal pain
options.E: Ongoing fetal movement

questions.rationale: Placenta previa typically presents with painless bright-red bleeding in the second half of pregnancy. Fetal movement may still be present, especially if fetal compromise has not yet developed. The absence of pain helps distinguish it from placental abruption in many cases.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Likely placenta previa requiring maternal-fetal assessment and bleeding precautions
options.B: Normal labour show
options.D: Postpartum haemorrhage

questions.rationale: The bleeding pattern strongly suggests placenta previa. Because placenta overlies or approaches the cervical os, vaginal bleeding may occur without pain. The nurse must think about safe assessment and preventing further bleeding.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Risk for maternal blood loss and fetal compromise related to placental bleeding
options.B: Disturbed body image
options.D: Readiness for discharge

questions.rationale: The immediate concern is ongoing bleeding and its impact on maternal circulation and fetal perfusion.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Assess maternal-fetal status, monitor bleeding, and avoid vaginal examination until placenta location is confirmed by the appropriate team
options.B: Perform a digital vaginal exam to check dilation
options.C: Encourage the patient to walk around
options.D: Delay fetal monitoring until bleeding stops

questions.rationale: In suspected placenta previa, digital vaginal examination may provoke severe bleeding and is contraindicated unless specifically directed in a controlled setting. Maternal and fetal monitoring are immediate priorities.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Monitor vital signs and bleeding amount closely
options.B: Apply fetal monitoring and assess fetal status
options.C: Prepare for ultrasound-based evaluation and possible admission
options.D: Explain the need for pelvic rest if ordered
options.E: Ignore maternal anxiety because bleeding is the only priority

questions.rationale: Maternity care is both physiological and supportive. Monitoring, fetal assessment, preparation for evaluation, and patient teaching are all appropriate. Anxiety should not be ignored.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates stable management at this stage?

options.A: Bleeding decreases or remains controlled, maternal vital signs stay stable, and fetal status remains reassuring
options.B: Bleeding increases while monitoring is reduced
options.C: A digital exam is performed without indication
options.D: The patient is discharged without ongoing assessment

questions.rationale: Stable maternal signs and reassuring fetal assessment indicate the situation is under better control, though continued vigilance is still needed.

caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Priya Menon, a 37-year-old multiparous woman at 35 weeks’ gestation, arrives complaining of sudden severe abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding after she slipped on wet flooring earlier in the day. She is guarding her abdomen and says the pain is constant. She reports reduced fetal movement since the pain began.
On assessment, the uterus feels firm and tender. Blood pressure is 96/60 mmHg, pulse 124 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and the fetal monitor shows a concerning pattern. The nurse suspects placental abruption.

questions.prompt: Which findings support placental abruption? Select all that apply.

options.A: Severe abdominal pain
options.B: Uterine tenderness and firmness
options.D: Reduced fetal movement
options.E: Signs of maternal instability

questions.rationale: Placental abruption typically presents with painful bleeding, uterine tenderness, and often reduced fetal movement due to compromised placental exchange. Maternal tachycardia and hypotension suggest significant blood loss or shock.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Normal labour discomfort
options.B: Placental abruption with risk of maternal haemorrhage and fetal compromise
options.D: Baby blues

questions.rationale: This is a painful bleeding emergency, unlike the typically painless bleeding seen with placenta previa. The nurse must recognise the dual risk to mother and fetus.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Impaired placental perfusion with maternal haemorrhage risk
options.B: Disturbed sleep pattern
options.D: Need for menu planning

questions.rationale: Placental separation compromises fetal oxygenation and may lead to severe maternal bleeding. This is a high-priority obstetric emergency.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Initiate urgent maternal-fetal assessment, support circulation, and prepare for emergency obstetric management
options.B: Encourage the patient to walk to the toilet
options.C: Delay fetal monitoring until the bleeding is measured for several hours
options.D: Offer oral food and fluids first

questions.rationale: The nurse must stabilise maternal circulation and monitor fetal status immediately. Delay or unnecessary activity would be unsafe.

questions.prompt: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Frequent monitoring of maternal vital signs and bleeding
options.B: Continuous fetal heart rate assessment
options.C: Preparation for urgent birth if maternal or fetal instability worsens
options.D: Maintaining IV access and readiness for rapid intervention as ordered
options.E: Assuming that reduced fetal movement is not important

questions.rationale: Reduced fetal movement is highly significant and should not be ignored. The nurse must prepare for escalation and possible urgent delivery.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates the patient is being effectively stabilised while definitive care is arranged?

options.A: Maternal perfusion is supported, fetal status is continuously assessed, and the team is prepared for rapid obstetric intervention
options.B: Monitoring is stopped because pain is present
options.D: The patient is left alone because the doctor has been called

questions.rationale: Effective emergency nursing care involves continuous assessment, support, and anticipation of urgent obstetric management.

caseStudies.caseStudyTitle: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour
caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Jasmine Thomas is in active labour at 39 weeks and is receiving oxytocin augmentation. Over the last 20 minutes the nurse notices repeated fetal heart rate decelerations that begin after the peak of each contraction and return to baseline after the contraction has ended.
The mother is anxious and tired. Maternal vital signs are stable, contractions are strong and regular, and the fetal strip shows a concerning pattern. The nurse recognises late decelerations as potentially indicating uteroplacental insufficiency.

questions.prompt: Which description best identifies late decelerations?

options.A: Decelerations that mirror the contraction exactly
options.B: Decelerations that begin after the contraction peak and recover after the contraction ends
options.C: Abrupt drops associated with cord compression
options.D: A reassuring fetal pattern

questions.rationale: Late decelerations start after the peak of the contraction and recover after it ends. This timing is the key identifying feature and usually reflects impaired uteroplacental perfusion.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation of repeated late decelerations?

options.A: Reassuring fetal adaptation
options.B: Fetal oxygenation concern related to uteroplacental insufficiency
options.D: Maternal anxiety only

questions.rationale: Late decelerations are abnormal because they suggest the fetus is not tolerating contractions well, often due to decreased oxygen transfer.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Potential fetal compromise due to reduced placental oxygen exchange
options.B: Maternal boredom
options.D: Room temperature discomfort

questions.rationale: The fetus is the most immediate concern here. The nurse must intervene to improve oxygen delivery and reduce stress on the fetus.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Reposition the mother, reduce or stop oxytocin as indicated by protocol, support oxygenation, and increase maternal-fetal assessment
options.B: Encourage the mother to push harder
options.C: Leave the oxytocin unchanged and ignore the tracing
options.D: Delay action until the next shift

questions.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation measures include maternal repositioning, addressing oxytocin-driven uterine stress, supporting oxygenation, and close monitoring. This is a classic NCLEX maternity priority question.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Assess maternal blood pressure and contraction pattern
options.B: Consider an IV fluid bolus if indicated or ordered
options.C: Notify the provider or midwife of the non-reassuring pattern
options.D: Continue to label the pattern as normal to calm the patient
options.E: Prepare for further intervention if the pattern persists

questions.rationale: The nurse must address reversible causes and escalate appropriately. Falsely labelling the pattern as normal would be unsafe and misleading.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates that the interventions are effective?

options.A: Late decelerations reduce or resolve and fetal tracing becomes more reassuring
options.B: Decelerations worsen while oxytocin continues unchanged
options.C: Fetal tracing is not reassessed after repositioning
options.D: The mother remains uninformed and distressed

questions.rationale: The goal of intervention is a more reassuring fetal pattern. The nurse must evaluate whether intrauterine resuscitation is working and escalate if it is not.

caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Catherine George is in labour at 38 weeks. Shortly after spontaneous rupture of membranes, the fetal heart rate suddenly drops deeply and does not recover normally. On rapid assessment, the nurse suspects umbilical cord prolapse.
The patient is frightened and asks what is happening. The fetal tracing remains concerning. The nurse understands that compression of the prolapsed cord can rapidly compromise fetal oxygenation and requires immediate action.

questions.prompt: Which findings suggest possible cord prolapse? Select all that apply.

options.A: Sudden fetal bradycardia after rupture of membranes
options.B: Abrupt severe decelerations
options.D: Ongoing non-reassuring fetal tracing
options.E: Need for rapid intrauterine resuscitation

questions.rationale: Cord prolapse is classically suspected when severe fetal heart rate compromise occurs immediately after rupture of membranes. The sequence of events is highly important in the diagnosis.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Reassuring labour progression
options.B: Probable umbilical cord compression/prolapse causing acute fetal hypoxia risk
options.D: Postpartum complication

questions.rationale: The problem is urgent fetal compromise from cord compression. NCLEX expects immediate recognition because delay can be catastrophic.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Acute interruption of fetal oxygen delivery due to cord compression
options.B: Maternal sleep deprivation
options.D: Breastfeeding readiness

questions.rationale: The fetus is at immediate risk because the compressed cord limits oxygenated blood flow.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Call for help, relieve pressure from the presenting part as indicated, reposition the patient urgently, and prepare for emergency birth
options.B: Leave the patient to find paperwork first
options.C: Encourage the patient to sit upright and push
options.D: Delay intervention until contractions slow

questions.rationale: Relieving cord compression and summoning urgent obstetric help are the priorities. Time is critical, and the nurse must act immediately.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Continuous fetal monitoring
options.B: Clear communication with the patient and team
options.C: Preparation for urgent operative birth if indicated
options.D: Maintaining interventions that reduce cord compression
options.E: Assuming the tracing will normalise without action

questions.rationale: Every minute matters in cord prolapse. Ongoing monitoring, communication, decompression, and preparation for emergency birth are all correct.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates that nursing management is helping while definitive delivery is arranged?

options.A: Fetal heart rate improves or is better maintained while pressure is relieved and the team prepares for urgent birth
options.B: Fetal tracing worsens while interventions are stopped
options.C: The patient is left uninformed and alone
options.D: No further monitoring is done after the first response

questions.rationale: Improved or better-maintained fetal status while emergency delivery is organised shows that decompression efforts are helping.

caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Amy Wilson is in the second stage of labour and the fetal head has just delivered. However, the head retracts tightly against the perineum and the shoulders fail to deliver with gentle downward guidance. The birth team quickly recognises possible shoulder dystocia.
The mother is exhausted and frightened, and the nurse must help coordinate the emergency response while understanding that forceful traction may injure both mother and infant.

questions.prompt: Which findings suggest shoulder dystocia? Select all that apply.

options.A: Head delivers but shoulders do not follow
options.B: Retraction of the fetal head against the perineum
options.D: Risk of fetal hypoxia and birth injury
options.E: Birth process suddenly stalls

questions.rationale: These findings strongly indicate shoulder dystocia. The retraction of the head, often called the turtle sign, is a classic cue.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Normal labour delay
options.B: Shoulder dystocia requiring immediate coordinated obstetric manoeuvres
options.D: Postpartum haemorrhage

questions.rationale: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency because the impacted shoulder can prevent delivery and compromise fetal oxygenation.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Risk for fetal hypoxia and traumatic birth injury
options.B: Maternal thirst
options.D: Sleep deprivation

questions.rationale: The urgency lies in relieving the shoulder impaction to allow delivery and prevent hypoxia or injury.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Call for help immediately and assist with emergency manoeuvres according to the provider’s direction
options.B: Pull forcefully on the fetal head
options.C: Leave the room to call family
options.D: Delay action until the next contraction

questions.rationale: Shoulder dystocia requires immediate team response and use of recognised manoeuvres. Forceful traction can cause serious injury and is inappropriate.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Provide clear, focused support to the mother
options.B: Prepare equipment and personnel for neonatal assessment after birth
options.C: Anticipate possible maternal trauma or postpartum bleeding after delivery
options.D: Assume the infant will always be fine after delivery
options.E: Maintain calm communication with the team

questions.rationale: The nurse must think beyond the moment of delivery and anticipate neonatal and maternal complications. Calm teamwork is essential.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates effective emergency management?

options.A: The infant is delivered, immediate neonatal assessment occurs, and the mother is assessed for trauma and bleeding
options.B: Delivery remains stalled with no coordinated response
options.C: The nurse stops monitoring after the infant is born
options.D: Maternal assessment is ignored after delivery

questions.rationale: Successful management includes safe delivery and immediate follow-up care for both mother and infant.

caseStudies.caseStudyTitle: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony
caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Riya Sharma has just delivered vaginally 30 minutes ago. The nurse notices that she is bleeding more heavily than expected, soaking pads rapidly. She says she feels weak and dizzy. On palpation, the uterus feels boggy and enlarged above the expected level.
Her blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg, pulse 122 beats per minute, and she appears pale. The nurse recognises likely postpartum haemorrhage caused by uterine atony.

questions.prompt: Which findings indicate postpartum haemorrhage with uterine atony? Select all that apply.

options.A: Heavy vaginal bleeding
options.B: Boggy enlarged uterus
options.D: Tachycardia and low blood pressure
options.E: Pallor

questions.rationale: These are hallmark findings of postpartum haemorrhage. A boggy uterus suggests uterine atony, one of the most common causes of PPH. Hemodynamic changes show significant blood loss.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Normal postpartum lochia
options.B: Postpartum haemorrhage likely caused by uterine atony
options.D: Normal fatigue after delivery

questions.rationale: This bleeding exceeds normal lochia and is associated with a soft, enlarged uterus and unstable vital signs. NCLEX maternity care requires rapid recognition of uterine atony as an emergency.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Risk for hypovolemic shock from postpartum blood loss
options.B: Sleep deprivation
options.D: Mild discomfort from contractions

questions.rationale: Severe blood loss threatens maternal perfusion and can lead quickly to shock. That is the immediate priority.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Massage the fundus, call for assistance, assess bleeding, and prepare uterotonic therapy as prescribed
options.B: Send the patient to shower
options.C: Delay action because bleeding is common after birth
options.D: Focus only on breastfeeding support

questions.rationale: Fundal massage and urgent support are initial priorities in uterine atony. The nurse must not minimise heavy bleeding because postpartum haemorrhage can deteriorate rapidly.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Monitor vital signs frequently
options.B: Evaluate bladder distention because a full bladder can worsen atony
options.C: Prepare IV fluids and medications as ordered
options.D: Continue to assess lochia and uterine tone
options.E: Ignore the patient’s dizziness if bleeding seems to slow briefly

questions.rationale: PPH requires repeated reassessment. Bladder distention can interfere with uterine contraction. Dizziness remains clinically important and should not be dismissed.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.A: The uterus becomes firm, bleeding decreases, vital signs begin to stabilise, and the patient feels less dizzy
options.B: The uterus remains boggy and bleeding continues
options.C: Monitoring stops because the fundus was massaged once
options.D: The patient becomes more hypotensive without escalation

questions.rationale: A firm fundus, reduced bleeding, and improved hemodynamic status show effective control of uterine atony.

caseStudies.narrative:
Mrs. Linda Fernandes is two days postpartum after a prolonged labour and operative vaginal birth. She now reports chills, lower abdominal pain, and foul-smelling lochia. She says she feels hot and unwell, and she winces when the uterus is palpated.
Her temperature is 38.8 C, pulse 112 beats per minute, and the uterus is tender. The nurse suspects postpartum endometritis.

questions.prompt: Which findings support endometritis? Select all that apply.

options.A: Fever
options.B: Uterine tenderness
options.D: Chills and malaise
options.E: Tachycardia

questions.rationale: All findings are consistent with postpartum uterine infection. Risk factors include prolonged labour and invasive or operative birth.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Normal postpartum healing
options.B: Postpartum endometritis requiring prompt treatment
options.D: Breast engorgement only

questions.rationale: The symptoms suggest uterine infection, not normal recovery. Prompt treatment is needed to prevent progression to sepsis.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Infection with risk of systemic spread
options.B: Disturbed sleep
options.D: Minor perineal discomfort

questions.rationale: The main concern is infection and possible systemic deterioration if untreated.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Assess thoroughly, obtain needed cultures as ordered, and prepare for prescribed antibiotic therapy while monitoring maternal status
options.B: Ignore the odour because lochia can vary
options.D: Delay treatment until fever is rechecked tomorrow

questions.rationale: The nurse should support timely diagnosis and treatment. Foul-smelling lochia and uterine tenderness are not normal findings to dismiss.

questions.prompt: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Monitor temperature and vital signs closely
options.B: Assess lochia and uterine tenderness trends
options.C: Encourage hydration and rest as clinically appropriate
options.D: Watch for worsening signs of sepsis
options.E: Ignore the patient’s pain if antibiotics are started

questions.rationale: Close monitoring remains important even after treatment starts. Pain and sepsis risk both require ongoing reassessment.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.A: Fever decreases, lochia becomes less offensive, uterine tenderness lessens, and the patient feels stronger
options.B: Fever rises and confusion develops
options.C: No reassessment occurs after antibiotics begin
options.D: Tachycardia worsens with ongoing pain

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by reduction in infection signs and better overall maternal wellbeing.

caseStudies.narrative:
A term male newborn is delivered after a prolonged labour. Five minutes after birth, the nurse notes persistent grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and central cyanosis despite routine drying and stimulation. The infant’s breathing appears laboured.
The mother asks whether this is normal. The nurse knows that while some transitional findings can be expected, this pattern indicates probable respiratory distress requiring immediate action.

questions.prompt: Which findings are concerning for significant newborn respiratory distress? Select all that apply.

options.A: Grunting
options.B: Nasal flaring
options.D: Central cyanosis
options.E: Laboured breathing

questions.rationale: All of these signs indicate increased work of breathing and poor oxygenation. Unlike benign transitional findings such as acrocyanosis, central cyanosis and significant respiratory effort are urgent.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Normal newborn transition only
options.B: Newborn respiratory distress requiring immediate assessment and support
options.D: Mild sleepiness

questions.rationale: This infant is not transitioning normally. The pattern strongly indicates respiratory compromise.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Impaired oxygenation and ineffective breathing in the newborn
options.B: Need for routine feeding
options.D: Bathing delay

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing always come first, especially in the newborn, who can deteriorate rapidly.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Initiate immediate newborn respiratory assessment and support according to neonatal protocol, and escalate urgently
options.B: Swaddle tightly and wait an hour
options.D: Assume cyanosis will resolve without reassessment

questions.rationale: The nurse must act immediately because this infant shows clear signs of respiratory distress. Delay may lead to severe hypoxia.

questions.prompt: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Maintain thermoregulation while respiratory support is organised
options.B: Reassess colour, respiratory effort, and oxygenation frequently
options.C: Communicate clearly with the parent while continuing urgent care
options.D: Observe for worsening grunting or apnea
options.E: Ignore retractions if the infant is term

questions.rationale: Respiratory distress management includes warmth, reassessment, communication, and observation for worsening fatigue or apnea. Term status does not make retractions normal.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.A: Colour improves, grunting decreases, breathing becomes easier, and the infant maintains better oxygenation
options.B: Cyanosis persists and respirations become weaker
options.C: Monitoring stops once the infant is quieter
options.D: The infant becomes more lethargic without escalation

questions.rationale: Improved work of breathing and oxygenation indicate effective early management.

caseStudies.narrative:
A late preterm infant born to a mother with gestational diabetes is being monitored in the postnatal unit. A few hours after birth, the infant becomes jittery, sleepy, and demonstrates poor feeding. The nurse checks the glucose result and finds it below the expected safe range for the newborn.
The infant is otherwise warm and pink but less vigorous than earlier. The nurse recognises newborn hypoglycaemia as a priority problem because the brain is highly sensitive to low glucose.

questions.prompt: Which findings support neonatal hypoglycaemia? Select all that apply.

options.A: Jitteriness
options.B: Poor feeding
options.D: Infant of a mother with gestational diabetes
options.E: Low glucose reading

questions.rationale: All of these factors support neonatal hypoglycaemia. Infants of diabetic mothers are at particular risk because of altered glucose-insulin adaptation after birth.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Normal newborn behaviour only
options.B: Neonatal hypoglycaemia requiring prompt treatment and reassessment
options.D: Benign sleep cycle

questions.rationale: Low glucose with symptoms must be treated promptly. Waiting risks worsening neurological compromise.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Inadequate glucose availability to the newborn brain
options.B: Need for routine discharge teaching
options.D: Delayed bathing

questions.rationale: In neonatal hypoglycaemia, neurological protection is the main priority.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Initiate feeding or other protocol-based glucose support promptly and reassess the infant closely
options.B: Delay action until the next routine blood sugar check
options.D: Ignore symptoms if the infant is warm

questions.rationale: Rapid correction and close reassessment are required. Hypoglycaemia should not be left untreated simply because the infant looks otherwise stable.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Maintain warmth and reduce energy expenditure
options.B: Recheck glucose after treatment according to protocol
options.D: Explain the situation calmly to the parents
options.E: Assume one low reading is never important

questions.rationale: Thermoregulation, repeat glucose testing, feeding assessment, and parent communication are all appropriate. A low symptomatic reading is always important.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.A: Glucose rises to a safer range, feeding improves, jitteriness resolves, and the infant becomes more alert
options.B: Lethargy worsens and feeding remains poor
options.D: The infant becomes weaker without escalation

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in both biochemical correction and clinical behaviour.

caseStudies.narrative:
A 3-day-old newborn is brought to the nursery for assessment because the mother notices increasing yellow discoloration of the skin and eyes. The infant is feeding but appears sleepier than on the previous day. The bilirubin result is above the safe threshold for the infant’s age and clinical context.
The nurse must assess severity, feeding adequacy, and risk of worsening jaundice while preparing for phototherapy and parent teaching if ordered.

questions.prompt: Which findings support clinically important neonatal jaundice? Select all that apply.

options.A: Yellow discoloration of skin and sclera
options.B: Increased sleepiness
options.D: Need to assess feeding pattern
options.E: Newborn age of 3 days

questions.rationale: All the listed points matter. Jaundice is common in newborns, but rising bilirubin plus sleepiness and feeding concerns can indicate a need for treatment and close monitoring.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: This can never be significant because jaundice is always normal
options.B: The infant may have clinically significant hyperbilirubinemia requiring monitoring and possibly phototherapy
options.D: The colour change is unrelated to bilirubin

questions.rationale: Physiologic jaundice may be common, but significant bilirubin elevation can be harmful. The nurse must assess severity and follow treatment thresholds.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Risk for bilirubin-related neurological injury if levels rise further
options.B: Disturbed sleep pattern of the parents
options.D: Umbilical cord stump education only

questions.rationale: Very high bilirubin can become dangerous, so preventing neurological injury is the priority.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Assess feeding and elimination, verify bilirubin trends, and prepare for phototherapy or other management as ordered
options.B: Delay all care until the next day
options.D: Ignore sleepiness if the infant is yellow

questions.rationale: Feeding and bilirubin trend assessment are crucial because poor intake can worsen jaundice. Delaying care or stopping feeds would be unsafe.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Monitor hydration and feeding effectiveness
options.B: Provide parent education about jaundice and phototherapy if used
options.D: Observe for worsening lethargy or poor feeding
options.E: Assume jaundice will always resolve without follow-up

questions.rationale: Safe newborn care includes monitoring, education, and follow-up. A passive wait-and-see approach is inappropriate when bilirubin is already elevated.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.A: Bilirubin trends down, feeding improves, and the infant is more alert
options.B: Sleepiness increases and feeding declines
options.C: Phototherapy is started but never reassessed
options.D: Parents remain uninformed about warning signs

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by falling bilirubin and better feeding/alertness.

caseStudies.narrative:
A newborn delivered after prolonged rupture of membranes becomes increasingly lethargic within the first day of life. The infant feeds poorly, has temperature instability, and shows periods of mottled skin and intermittent grunting. The mother asks why the baby seems less responsive than immediately after birth.
The nurse understands that newborn sepsis may present subtly and can deteriorate rapidly. The infant requires urgent assessment and escalation.

questions.prompt: Which findings raise concern for neonatal sepsis? Select all that apply.

options.A: Poor feeding
options.B: Lethargy
options.D: Mottling and grunting
options.E: Prolonged rupture of membranes

questions.rationale: All these findings are concerning. Neonatal sepsis often presents with non-specific signs, so nurses must respond quickly to subtle deterioration.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Normal newborn tiredness
options.B: Possible neonatal sepsis requiring urgent evaluation and treatment
options.D: Benign adaptation

questions.rationale: The symptom cluster plus prolonged rupture of membranes makes infection a serious concern.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Risk for overwhelming infection and respiratory compromise in the newborn
options.B: Need for discharge teaching
options.D: Parent inconvenience

questions.rationale: Newborn sepsis can become life-threatening quickly. The priority is survival and prevention of rapid decline.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Escalate urgently, support thermoregulation and respiratory assessment, and prepare for sepsis evaluation and treatment as ordered
options.B: Wait to see whether the infant perks up after sleep
options.C: Stop monitoring because the baby is quiet
options.D: Feed only when convenient later

questions.rationale: Urgent action is required because newborn sepsis may progress rapidly. Thermoregulation and respiratory support are important immediate priorities.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Monitor colour, tone, respirations, and feeding closely
options.B: Support family understanding while urgent care continues
options.C: Anticipate cultures and antibiotic therapy as ordered
options.D: Ignore grunting if the infant is term
options.E: Reassess temperature and perfusion frequently

questions.rationale: Close observation and family communication are important. Grunting is a serious respiratory sign and must not be ignored.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.A: Feeding improves, colour and tone stabilise, temperature becomes more consistent, and respiratory effort eases
options.B: Lethargy deepens and grunting worsens
options.D: Perfusion is not reassessed

questions.rationale: Improvement must be seen in behaviour, temperature, perfusion, and breathing.

caseStudies.caseStudyTitle: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome
caseStudies.narrative:
A 32-week preterm infant is admitted to the neonatal care area shortly after birth. The nurse observes tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, and subcostal retractions. The infant is small, has minimal respiratory reserve, and requires support to maintain temperature and oxygenation.
The mother is anxious and asks whether the baby will be able to breathe independently. The nurse recognises the pattern as consistent with respiratory distress syndrome related to prematurity.

questions.prompt: Which findings support respiratory distress syndrome in a preterm infant? Select all that apply.

options.A: Prematurity at 32 weeks
options.B: Tachypnoea
options.D: Retractions
options.E: Reduced physiological reserve

questions.rationale: Prematurity strongly predisposes to surfactant deficiency and RDS. The visible work of breathing confirms respiratory compromise.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Normal newborn transition only
options.B: Respiratory distress syndrome requiring close support of breathing and thermoregulation
options.D: Stable sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The infant’s prematurity and clear respiratory distress signs indicate RDS rather than normal transition.

questions.prompt: Which problem is most urgent?

options.A: Impaired gas exchange and risk of worsening fatigue in the premature infant
options.B: Need for routine cord teaching only
options.D: Delayed naming ceremony

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing are always first, especially in preterm infants who fatigue quickly.

questions.prompt: What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Support airway and breathing according to neonatal protocol, maintain thermoregulation, and escalate for advanced neonatal management
options.B: Delay intervention to allow longer skin-to-skin time only
options.D: Ignore the grunting because preterm infants are noisy

questions.rationale: The infant requires respiratory and thermal support immediately. Delay may worsen hypoxia and exhaustion.

questions.prompt: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.A: Reassess colour, work of breathing, and oxygenation frequently
options.B: Minimise energy expenditure and unnecessary stimulation
options.C: Support parent understanding while urgent care continues
options.D: Prepare for neonatal respiratory support measures as ordered
options.E: Assume the infant will self-correct without reassessment

questions.rationale: A preterm infant with RDS needs close reassessment, energy conservation, and timely escalation. Parent communication remains important.

questions.prompt: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.A: Respiratory effort lessens, oxygenation improves, and the infant maintains temperature and colour more effectively
options.B: Retractions worsen and the infant becomes more lethargic
options.C: Monitoring stops once the infant is quieter
options.D: Temperature falls further without action

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by easier breathing, better oxygenation, and more stable thermal control.
